card.title: One class, many objects
card.blurb: Make several objects from one class and watch them appear in memory, each with its own values.
hero.title: One class, many objects
intro.0: You have written a class and made an object from it. So how many objects can one class make?
intro.1: It is easy to read a class as if it were the thing itself - one Cat class, one cat. That reading holds up until the day you need a second cat, and then everything you hardcoded inside the class turns out to be shared by every cat you make.
intro.2: Here you write the code and watch memory while it runs. Each new puts another object on screen, side by side, each with its own values - which is the difference between the blueprint and the things built from it.
task.1.title: Three cats from one class
task.1.context:
One class can make as many objects as you ask for. Each `new Cat(...)` sets aside its own slot in memory, so three cats are three separate things - not three names for one thing. Two of them can even share a name and still be different cats; what separates them is the slot, not the label.

The code below makes one cat. Make two more, each with a different name, and describe all three. Then press Visualize and watch the right-hand side: you are looking for three cards, not one.
task.1.goal.0: Three Cat objects exist at the same time.
task.1.goal.1: All three cats hold different names.
task.2.title: What the constructor does
task.2.context:
`new Cat("Ana", 3)` is not one thing - it is two. First a blank object is set aside, then a method runs to fill it in. That method is the constructor, and its job is to copy what the caller passed into the object's own fields.

This constructor has been left empty, so all three cats come out identical no matter what `Main` passes. Fill it in. Then Visualize and step through: you will see the `Cat` frame open on the stack, do its work, and close again - once per cat.
task.2.goal.0: The three cats end up with different names.
task.2.goal.1: The three cats end up with different ages.
task.3.title: The values you pass in
task.3.context:
The values in the brackets are `arguments`. The names in the constructor's own brackets are `parameters`. When the constructor runs, each argument is copied into the parameter sitting in the same position - first to first, second to second. That is the whole rule, and it is why order matters.

Make three robots with different batteries. Visualize it, step onto the `Robot` frame, and read the parameters: they hold whatever that particular `new` passed.
task.3.goal.1: The three robots hold different battery levels.
task.4.title: A parameter only lives inside its method
task.4.context:
An ordinary method takes arguments the same way a constructor does. `Add(3)` copies `3` into the parameter `amount`, and `amount` exists only while `Add` is running - it appears on the stack when the call starts and is gone when the call returns.

Write the body of `Add`, then add a third call so the total comes to 9. Visualize it and watch the stack: `amount` shows up three times, holding a different number each time, and never outlives its call.
task.5.title: Which object is the method running on?
task.5.context:
`tally.Add(2)` names two things: the method to run, and the object to run it on. One `Add` is written once and shared by every counter, but each call reaches into the fields of the one object in front of the dot.

Make a second counter and add a different amount to it. Visualize it: the same `Add` frame opens twice, and each time the arrow points at a different counter - so the two totals never mix.
task.5.goal.0: Two Counter objects exist at the same time.
task.5.goal.1: The two counters hold different totals.
concept.pr-instance.def: One object made from a class. Several instances of one class each hold their own values.
task.6.summaryIntro: A class is the shape; each `new` makes another object with that shape and its own values. You did not take any of it on trust - every card you watched appear came from your own code actually running.
task.6.summaryItems.0.title: Instance -
task.6.summaryItems.0.text: one object made from a class. Three calls to `new Cat(...)` make three, and each keeps its own values.
task.6.summaryItems.1.title: Constructor -
task.6.summaryItems.1.text: the method `new` runs to fill the fresh object in. It runs once per object, then its frame closes.
task.6.summaryItems.2.title: Argument and parameter -
task.6.summaryItems.2.text: the value you pass, and the name it lands in. They pair up by position, so the order in the brackets is the order they arrive in.
task.6.summaryItems.3.title: Local scope -
task.6.summaryItems.3.text: a parameter exists only while its method is running. It appears on the stack with the call and is gone when the call returns.
task.6.summaryItems.4.title: The receiver -
task.6.summaryItems.4.text: the object in front of the dot. One method is written once, but each call reads and writes the fields of that one object.
task.6.summaryClose: Next you will give a class more than one way to be built, and see why the constructor is the place a rule about the object belongs.
